item.title: The Party Wall Trap Catching Out London Landlords Mid-Renovation
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

For landlords in London looking to maximise rental yields, property renovations such as loft conversions or rear extensions can be highly effective strategies. These upgrades often increase a property’s value and appeal to tenants. However, amidst the focus on surveys, structural repairs, and compliance, one crucial aspect is frequently overlooked: the Party Wall Act 1996. Failure to adhere to this legislation can lead to costly delays and disputes, catching many landlords off-guard mid-renovation.

What Is the Party Wall Act?

The Party Wall Act is a piece of legislation designed to prevent and resolve disputes between neighbours when building work involves shared walls, boundaries, or structures. In London, where terraced houses and flats are common, this law is particularly relevant. It requires homeowners and landlords to notify adjoining property owners if planned work falls within the Act’s scope. This includes excavations near neighbouring buildings, building on the boundary line, or altering shared walls.

Landlords might assume that obtaining planning permission and building regulations approval covers all legal requirements. However, the Party Wall Act operates independently, and overlooking it can result in formal disputes, delays, and even fines. Ignorance of the law is not a valid defence, making it essential for landlords to familiarise themselves with its provisions before starting any renovation project.

Common Pitfalls for London Landlords

One of the most frequent mistakes landlords make is failing to serve the correct notice to neighbours. Under the Act, written notice must be provided at least two months before work begins. This notice should detail the proposed work and its potential impact on adjoining properties. If neighbours raise concerns, a Party Wall Agreement must be drawn up, often involving a surveyor to mediate and ensure fairness.

Another common oversight is underestimating the time required to navigate the Party Wall process. Delays can occur if neighbours dispute the work or if paperwork is not handled correctly. For landlords working to tight renovation schedules, these delays can be costly, potentially leading to lost rental income.

Additionally, some landlords may mistakenly believe that minor works, such as installing shelves or replastering, are exempt from the Act. While certain small-scale projects do fall outside its scope, it is always advisable to seek professional advice to confirm whether the Act applies.

How to Avoid the Party Wall Trap

To avoid falling foul of the Party Wall Act, landlords might consider consulting a specialist surveyor or solicitor early in the planning process. These professionals can help determine whether the Act applies to the proposed work and ensure that all necessary notices are served correctly.

Open communication with neighbours is also key. By discussing plans in advance and addressing any concerns, landlords can often prevent disputes from arising. If neighbours do raise objections, engaging a qualified surveyor to mediate can help resolve issues efficiently.

Finally, landlords should factor the Party Wall process into their project timelines. Allocating extra time for potential delays can help ensure renovations stay on track and minimise disruption to tenants or rental income.

Whilst the Party Wall Act may seem like an additional hurdle, understanding and complying with it is essential for a smooth renovation process. By taking proactive steps, landlords in London can avoid the pitfalls of this legislation and focus on enhancing their property’s value and appeal.

item.title: Tiger Financial Outlines How Lenders Are Assessing Modular Housing Schemes in the UK
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The mortgage landscape for modular housing in the UK continues to evolve as lenders refine their approach to this modern construction method. With offsite-built homes gaining traction amongst developers and homebuyers alike, understanding lender criteria has become crucial for those considering this property type.

How Lenders Evaluate Modular Home Schemes

Specialist finance brokers report that underwriters typically scrutinise modular housing applications through several key lenses. Lenders commonly assess the manufacturer's track record, build quality certifications, and structural warranties before approving finance. Many favour modular properties constructed by firms with extensive experience and third-party accreditation from bodies like the British Standards Institution.

Underwriters also examine the transport and assembly process, as modular units must meet the same durability standards as traditional builds once installed. Financial institutions may request detailed technical specifications and site assembly plans to evaluate the project's viability. The permanence of foundations and connection to utilities often forms part of this assessment.

Financing Options for Modular Properties

Mortgage products for modular homes have become more widely available, though criteria still vary between lenders. Some high street banks now offer standard residential mortgages for certified modular properties, particularly those from established manufacturers. Developers might consider specialist development finance options during the construction phase, with some lenders providing bridging loans specifically for modular projects.

Prospective buyers should note that lender valuations for modular properties may differ from traditional homes. Valuers typically consider factors such as the property's integration into its plot, long-term maintenance requirements, and local market demand for this housing type. Obtaining a mortgage valuation from a surveyor experienced with modular construction could help streamline the financing process.

As modular construction becomes more mainstream in the UK property market, lenders continue to adapt their criteria. Homebuyers and developers may wish to consult specialist brokers familiar with both modular construction and lender requirements to navigate the financing process effectively. With proper planning and professional advice, modular homes can represent a viable route to homeownership or property investment.

item.title: Renters’ Rights Act risks creating two-tier rental market, Goodlord warns
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The Renters' Reform Bill may be creating a two-tier rental market as landlords and letting agents grow increasingly selective about tenants, according to new research from property technology firm Goodlord. Their annual State of the Lettings Industry report suggests recent legislative changes are making housing providers more cautious when assessing applications.

Landlords Adopt More Selective Approach

Goodlord's survey of over 3,000 industry professionals and tenants reveals shifting attitudes in the private rental sector. Some 51% of letting agents now exercise greater caution when recommending tenants compared to a year ago, while 26% of landlords admit they're rejecting applicants they might previously have accepted.

Nearly a third (31%) of landlords would rather leave properties vacant than accept tenants they perceive as higher risk. Goodlord's chief executive William Reeve warns this could create "a gulf between those settled in their properties and those seeking a new place to call home," with students, foreign nationals and those with non-traditional incomes potentially facing greater challenges.

Industry Sentiment Shows Mixed Picture

Despite these concerns, overall optimism in the lettings sector has improved year-on-year. The proportion of letting agents describing themselves as pessimistic fell from 48% to 40%, with larger agencies (42%) appearing more confident than smaller operators (28%).

Reeve suggests this divide may reflect larger firms' greater capacity to adapt to regulatory changes. However, landlords remain predominantly pessimistic, with 69% expressing negative views - albeit an improvement from 78% in the previous survey. Portfolio landlords with six or more properties show particularly low confidence levels at 81%.

Tenants, meanwhile, appear to be growing more optimistic about the rental market, though the research didn't specify exact figures for this group.

While these findings reflect reported intentions rather than actual rejection rates, they highlight how legislative changes can influence housing providers' risk assessments. Prospective tenants may wish to be aware that some landlords are becoming more selective, particularly regarding financial stability and tenancy duration expectations.

item.title: More landlords freeze rents as tenant affordability concerns grow
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Recent research by the TDS Charitable Foundation has revealed that a growing number of landlords in England are opting to freeze rents, with 50% choosing not to increase payments over the past year. This marks a significant rise from 39% in the previous year’s survey, highlighting a shift in landlord behaviour amidst rising concerns about tenant affordability and retention.

Tenant Retention and Affordability Concerns Drive Rent Freezes

For many landlords, retaining reliable tenants has become a priority. Among those who chose not to raise rents, 47% cited tenant retention as their primary reason, while 44% expressed concerns about tenants’ ability to cope with the rising cost of living. This trend was particularly evident among landlords without mortgages or those owning a single rental property. Additionally, landlords who had never used letting agents were also more likely to keep rents steady.

However, nearly half of the landlords surveyed (48%) did increase rents at least once in the past year. Higher running costs, maintenance expenses, and broader inflationary pressures were the most common reasons given for these rises. Landlords with larger portfolios, those earning £100,000 or more, and those managing houses in multiple occupation (HMOs) were more likely to impose rent increases.

Landlords Take a Pragmatic Approach to Rent Arrears

The survey also explored how landlords respond when tenants fall behind on rent payments. Around 26% of landlords reported having at least one tenant in arrears, a slight decrease from 29% the previous year. Rather than resorting to immediate enforcement action, many landlords preferred to work collaboratively with tenants to resolve financial difficulties.

Approximately 42% of landlords reported discussing payment issues directly with tenants, while 39% provided information about tenants’ rights or available support services. Additionally, 21% agreed to repayment plans, and 17% offered rent-free or reduced-rent periods to help tenants manage their financial challenges.

Balancing Act for Landlords

Dr Jennifer Harris, head of policy, research and social impact at The Dispute Service Group, noted that the findings reflect the competing pressures faced by landlords. “It is encouraging to see more landlords choosing to keep rents unchanged, particularly at a time when tenants are facing significant financial strain,” she said. “However, landlords themselves are grappling with rising costs, which can make balancing affordability and profitability a challenge.”

The research underscores the complexities of the rental market, where landlords must navigate tenant affordability concerns alongside their own financial pressures. As the cost-of-living crisis continues, both landlords and tenants may need to find new ways to work together to maintain stability in the rental sector.

item.title: landlord Law Newsround #459
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords face mounting challenges in rental market

Recent developments in the private rental sector highlight growing pressures on landlords, from tribunal rent challenges to accessibility demands and new regulatory requirements. With tenants becoming more informed about their rights, property owners may need to reassess their approach to tenancy management.

Evidence crucial in rent tribunal cases

Landlords facing rent challenges at tribunal hearings must provide clear, documented evidence to support their rental valuations. Research by Propertymark reveals significant regional variations in how tribunals assess accommodation standards, with particular scrutiny on floor areas, room dimensions and overall living space.

A recent Manchester case saw a tribunal actually reduce the rent below the existing charged amount. These decisions don't create binding precedents, meaning each case stands on its own merits based on the evidence presented. Landlords might consider maintaining comprehensive records including:

  • Detailed property measurements
  • Comparable local rental valuations
  • Documentation of any outstanding repairs
  • Records of property improvements

Rising demand for accessible rental properties

The shortage of accessible homes is creating difficulties for both tenants and landlords. Research indicates 38% of tenants feel anxious about requesting property adaptations, with concerns including:

  • Potential refusal by landlords (46%)
  • Property suitability for modifications (36%)
  • Funding for necessary work (28%)

This accessibility crisis has wider implications, costing the NHS and care providers an estimated £3.9 billion annually when patients cannot be discharged to unsuitable homes. Housing association Habinteg is urging local authorities to establish single points of contact to advise on adaptation funding before situations become critical.

New landlord database catches many unaware

A surprising 77% of landlords appear unaware of the forthcoming Private Rented Sector database, set for phased implementation from December. This mandatory register carries significant penalties for non-compliance, including:

  • Fines ranging from £7,000 to £40,000
  • Potential criminal prosecution
  • Prohibition on property advertising

With such substantial consequences, landlords may wish to familiarise themselves with the new requirements well in advance of the rollout. The property sector is calling for clearer communication from government to ensure all landlords understand their obligations under this scheme.

These developments highlight the evolving landscape of private rentals, where landlords must balance tenant rights with regulatory compliance. Staying informed and maintaining thorough records could prove essential for navigating these challenges successfully.

item.title: The UK property market is dead… isn’t it?
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Despite frequent headlines suggesting a downturn, the UK property market continues to show resilience. Homes are still being sold, buyers remain active, and people are moving, albeit in a challenging environment. Whilst estate agents may feel the pressure, the underlying statistics reveal a more nuanced picture. By delving into the numbers, it becomes clear that the market is far from stagnant, though it demands strategic approaches from both sellers and agents.

Understanding the Numbers

Recent data highlights that the property market is experiencing fluctuations, but not collapse. In Week 41, there were 32,200 new listings, slightly down from 33,000 the previous week. Year-to-date figures show 1.471 million new listings, which is marginally lower than 2025 but higher than both 2024 and pre-pandemic averages. This suggests a steady flow of properties entering the market.

Gross residential sales for Week 41 stood at 22,400 homes sold subject to contract (STC), a small dip from 22,600 the week before. Year-to-date, 989,000 UK homes have been sold STC. Whilst this is 7.5% lower than 2025, it remains higher than 2023 and pre-Covid levels. Net sales, accounting for fall-throughs, also show a positive trend, with 761,000 net home sales year-to-date, surpassing 2023 and pre-pandemic averages.

Challenges and Opportunities for Estate Agents

The current market landscape presents both challenges and opportunities for estate agents. Overvaluing properties, delaying price reductions, and lacking a clear post-listing strategy can hinder sellers' chances of moving. Agents who adapt their approach to align with market realities are more likely to succeed.

A case study in Burnley illustrates this point. Analysing local estate agents revealed significant differences in who achieves better prices and helps homeowners move more effectively. Agents who focus on realistic pricing, timely adjustments, and robust marketing strategies tend to outperform their competitors. This approach could serve as a model for agents across the UK looking to demonstrate their value in a tough market.

Whilst the market may not be as buoyant as in previous years, it remains active. Homeowners may wish to work with agents who employ data-driven strategies and prioritise their clients' needs. Borrowers might also consider reviewing their mortgage options to ensure they are well-positioned to navigate the current landscape.

In summary, the UK property market is far from "dead." Whilst challenges persist, opportunities abound for those willing to adapt and innovate. By focusing on realistic valuations, timely adjustments, and effective strategies, both sellers and agents can navigate this complex environment successfully.

item.title: Landlords face £170,000 nightmare after court orders return of alleged Airbnb subletter
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Two overseas landlords have reportedly lost nearly £170,000 in legal fees and lost rental income after their London properties were allegedly sublet as unauthorised holiday lets without their knowledge. The case highlights the potential risks for property owners who rely on third-party management services.

Unauthorised short-term lets discovered

Hong Kong-based landlords Eugene Chan and Herman Lee instructed an estate agent to sell their London flats in Angel and Holborn in May 2024. Rather than being marketed for sale, both properties allegedly appeared on multiple short-term rental platforms including Airbnb, with nightly rates reaching £478. The owners only discovered the situation when contacted by someone claiming to have rented one property for eight months.

The landlords allege they never authorised any lettings arrangement, despite their former estate agent - director of the now-dissolved Nest Estate Consultancy - having suggested temporary rentals when the properties initially failed to sell. By the time the owners regained possession in October 2024, they had reportedly incurred £84,000 in legal costs and lost approximately £87,000 in rental income.

Complex legal battle ensues

The situation became more complex when the landlords changed the locks after discovering the suspected unauthorised subletting. The individual claiming to be the tenant obtained court orders requiring the owners to restore access, launching separate proceedings in two county courts alleging unlawful eviction.

Legal professionals note the case demonstrates the risks of landlords taking direct action, even when disputing a tenancy's validity. The owners eventually secured possession orders through Section 8 notices citing rent arrears, but the process took nearly two years from initial discovery to regaining control of the properties.

  • £84,000 in legal costs incurred
  • £87,000 in lost rental income
  • Two-year duration to regain possession
  • £88,000 rent arrears ordered (recovery uncertain)

Growing concerns over property management risks

Solicitors report increasing enquiries about similar cases, particularly involving prime London properties and homes near transport hubs. The case serves as a cautionary tale for landlords, especially those managing properties remotely. Property owners might consider conducting regular checks on their investments and ensuring robust contracts with any managing agents.

While the court ordered the tenant to pay substantial arrears and costs, legal experts note recovery can prove challenging in such situations. The case underscores the importance of thorough due diligence when appointing property managers and maintaining clear communication channels regarding any lettings arrangements.

item.title: Estate agents losing a third of working day chasing property deals
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

New research reveals that UK estate agents spend over a third of their working hours chasing updates on property transactions. According to Landmark Information Group, professionals across the sector estimate dedicating 34% of their time to following up on outstanding information and responding to enquiries. The findings highlight growing inefficiencies in the home-moving process, with 74% of respondents reporting that increasing transaction fall-through rates are significantly impacting business performance.

Communication breakdowns delay transactions

Lengthy transaction timescales remain the top frustration for estate agents, with 41% citing delays as a major concern - up from 32% in previous research. Poor communication between parties has become nearly twice as problematic, with dissatisfaction jumping from 19% to 36%. Industry professionals identified two key solutions: 72% believe improvements to upfront property information would boost productivity, while 67% argue for better communication and transparency throughout the sales process.

The administrative burden appears to be worsening, with agents increasingly tied up managing expectations rather than progressing sales. Many suggest that gathering essential property information before marketing could prevent many common delays, allowing professionals to focus on moving transactions forward rather than resolving preventable issues.

Buyers face uncertainty and stress

The research also uncovered significant challenges for home movers, with 73% wishing they'd known more about a property or its location before making an offer. After agreeing a sale, 67% experienced uncertainty or delays that led to practical difficulties: 52% reported increased stress levels, 46% struggled to plan their moving date, and 33% faced unexpected costs or financial disruption.

Nearly all respondents (95%) believed access to comprehensive property information at the listing stage would reduce stress, while 92% wanted all parties involved to work from the same set of data. These findings suggest that improving transparency early in the process could benefit everyone involved in property transactions.

Industry calls for homebuying reforms

The research emerges as the government considers reforms to the homebuying process, with 81% of property professionals believing changes are long overdue. Some 71% expect that introducing earlier commitments from buyers and sellers could bring significant improvements to the system.

As the industry braces for potential reforms, the research highlights how better preparation and communication could transform the home-moving experience for professionals and consumers alike. With the right changes, the property market could see reduced fall-through rates, shorter transaction times and less stress for all parties involved.

item.title: Conveyancing stuck in the email age as government pushes home-buying reforms
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK property market continues to grapple with outdated practices, as new research reveals most conveyancers still rely on email for exchanging crucial documents. According to InfoTrack's Digital Conveyancing Maturity Index, a striking 70% of professionals use email to share pre-completion paperwork, with 65% managing deadlines through manual spreadsheets or similar systems.

Digital adoption lags behind government ambitions

These findings emerge as the government prepares sweeping reforms aimed at modernising property transactions. The proposed changes include digital property records, upfront information packs and legally binding contracts earlier in the process. However, the research suggests the industry may struggle to implement these reforms without significant operational changes.

LawtechUK, a Ministry of Justice-backed initiative, has warned that conveyancers need to accelerate their digital transformation. Chris Grant, a panel member at LawtechUK, emphasised that successful reforms depend on "trusted information being available earlier and moving reliably between parties" - something current systems often fail to achieve.

Mixed progress in conveyancing technology

The research reveals some positive developments in digital adoption:

  • 89% of firms now use digital identity verification (up from 76% in 2024)
  • 74% employ digital source-of-funds checks (compared to 57% previously)
  • 88% utilise case management systems

Despite these advances, traditional methods persist in key areas. Half of conveyancers still handle enquiries via post or email, while only 15% use shared digital workspaces to manage transactions between parties. This disconnect suggests many firms have invested in piecemeal digital solutions without fully transforming their workflows.

Experts highlight that successful reform requires coordinated action across the industry. Software providers must improve data sharing capabilities, lenders need to clarify when digital information can be accepted, and professional bodies should provide clearer guidance. Conveyancing firms themselves may wish to review how they exchange information with other parties in property transactions.

As the government moves forward with its modernisation plans, the property industry faces increasing pressure to leave behind email-based processes and embrace truly digital solutions. The coming years could prove pivotal in determining whether these reforms deliver their promised benefits of faster, more transparent home purchases.

item.title: Tenant refusing access? When landlords can ask the court to intervene
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords often face the challenge of arranging essential property inspections, only to find their tenants refusing access. This can be particularly problematic when it comes to mandatory checks, such as gas and electrical safety inspections, which are legal requirements. Gas safety inspections must be conducted annually, whilst electrical inspections in England are required at least every five years. But what options are available to landlords when tenants deny entry?

Understanding the Legal Framework

The case of Bromford Housing Association v. Robinson [2026] EWCC 61 highlights the legal complexities landlords may encounter when tenants refuse access. Although this case involved a housing association, its findings are relevant to private landlords too. Bromford needed to carry out a five-year electrical inspection, having last completed one in September 2021. Despite multiple attempts to arrange the inspection between June and August 2026, the tenant repeatedly denied access.

Bromford carried out a proportionality and Equality Act assessment before applying for an injunction. This sought to compel the tenant to allow access and authorised forced entry if compliance was not met. The tenant did not attend the hearing, leaving the court to consider three key issues:

  • The Electrical Safety Standards Regulations 2020, which mandate inspections. However, the judge noted that landlords who take all reasonable steps to comply are not considered in breach if tenants refuse access. This raised questions about whether a landlord could rely on statutory duty to justify an injunction.
  • The tenancy agreement, which included a clause requiring the tenant to permit inspections. The judge ruled that this clause covered electrical inspections, meaning the tenant was in breach of their agreement.
  • Section 11(6) of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985, which obliges tenants to allow access for property inspections at reasonable times, provided 24 hours’ written notice is given.

Steps Landlords Can Take

When faced with a tenant refusing access, landlords may wish to first review the tenancy agreement. Many agreements include clauses requiring tenants to permit inspections for safety checks and repairs. If such a clause exists, landlords could remind tenants of their contractual obligations.

If reminders prove ineffective, landlords might consider seeking legal advice. In cases where mandatory inspections are being obstructed, applying for an injunction could be a viable option. This would compel the tenant to allow access and, if necessary, authorise forced entry. However, landlords must ensure they follow correct procedures, including providing adequate notice and conducting proportionality assessments where required.

It’s also worth noting that landlords who take all reasonable steps to comply with legal obligations may not be held in breach if tenants refuse access. However, this does not absolve landlords of their duty to ensure the property remains safe and compliant with regulations.

Ultimately, communication and understanding the legal framework are crucial. By taking proactive steps and seeking professional guidance when needed, landlords can navigate these challenges effectively whilst fulfilling their responsibilities.

item.title: EPC C by 2030: Where Windows Fit in a Landlord’s £10,000 Upgrade Budget
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

With the UK government’s target for all rental properties to achieve an Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) rating of C or above by 2030, landlords are increasingly looking at ways to improve energy efficiency. For many, upgrading windows is often a top priority. Not only can new windows enhance a property’s appearance, but they also play a crucial role in reducing heat loss and improving comfort for tenants.

Why Windows Matter for Energy Efficiency

In older properties, particularly Victorian terraces, original single-glazed sash windows are often a significant source of heat loss. Draughty windows can lead to higher energy bills for tenants and make it harder for landlords to meet EPC requirements. Replacing these with modern double or triple-glazed windows can improve insulation, reduce condensation, and boost the property’s overall energy efficiency rating.

Whilst windows are a visible and impactful upgrade, landlords might also consider other improvements to meet the EPC C target. Insulating walls and roofs, upgrading boilers, and installing smart thermostats can all contribute to a more energy-efficient home. However, windows remain a popular starting point due to their immediate impact on both aesthetics and comfort.

Balancing Upgrades Within a Budget

For landlords with a £10,000 budget, prioritising upgrades is essential. Whilst window replacements can be costly, they often deliver a strong return on investment by improving tenant satisfaction and reducing energy costs. Landlords may wish to obtain quotes from multiple installers to ensure they get the best value for money.

It’s also worth exploring whether additional energy efficiency measures, such as loft insulation or draught-proofing, can be combined with window upgrades. These smaller improvements can be more cost-effective and still contribute significantly to achieving a higher EPC rating.

Long-Term Benefits of Energy Efficiency

Investing in energy-efficient upgrades not only helps landlords comply with future regulations but also increases the appeal of their properties to tenants. With rising energy costs, tenants are increasingly prioritising homes that are warm, comfortable, and cost-effective to heat. By improving a property’s EPC rating, landlords can attract and retain tenants more easily.

Furthermore, energy-efficient properties may command higher rental prices, offering landlords a potential increase in income over time. Whilst the initial outlay for upgrades can be significant, the long-term benefits often outweigh the costs.

As the 2030 deadline approaches, landlords may wish to start planning their energy efficiency improvements now. Upgrading windows is a practical and impactful step, but combining this with other measures can help achieve the EPC C target more effectively. By investing in their properties, landlords can ensure compliance, enhance tenant satisfaction, and potentially boost rental income in the years to come.

item.title: Rents keep climbing as landlords warn rising costs are squeezing supply
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

UK rental prices continue to outpace property price growth, with fresh data highlighting growing pressures in the private rented sector. The latest Office for National Statistics figures reveal a 3.8% annual increase in private rents across the UK as of September 2023, matching August's peak growth rate. In England alone, rents rose by 4%, whilst annual house price inflation slowed to just 0.9% in August.

Landlords facing mounting cost pressures

Industry experts suggest rising rents reflect landlords passing on increased expenses rather than profiteering. Property professionals highlight multiple financial pressures including higher mortgage rates, potential energy efficiency upgrades and regulatory uncertainty. Knight Frank's head of UK residential research notes that landlords are adjusting rents to account for potential void periods, possession proceedings and upcoming Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards requirements.

The buy-to-let market has become particularly challenging following 14 consecutive Bank of England base rate increases. Many landlords now face significantly higher mortgage payments when remortgaging, alongside growing maintenance and compliance costs. Some property owners report profit margins being squeezed to levels that make continued investment questionable.

Rental supply concerns persist

Despite strong tenant demand, property professionals warn that insufficient new investment is entering the private rented sector. Rightmove data indicates rental supply remains constrained, especially in London and other high-demand areas. Experts suggest the combination of higher borrowing costs and increased operational expenses has made buy-to-let less attractive to new investors.

Some established landlords are reportedly considering alternative strategies, including:

  • Exploring houses in multiple occupation (HMO) opportunities
  • Focusing on property refurbishment to increase yields
  • Reassessing portfolios based on long-term performance

Industry voices caution that without fresh investment, the supply-demand imbalance could persist, maintaining upward pressure on rental prices. The situation may be particularly challenging for tenants already struggling with cost-of-living pressures, as higher rents compound financial difficulties.

As the market evolves, both landlords and tenants face complex challenges. Whilst some areas show signs of balancing, fundamental supply issues combined with rising operating costs suggest rental affordability may remain under strain in the coming months.

item.title: Prime London house prices fall 7% as sellers slash asking prices
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Prime London property prices experienced a notable decline in September, with figures showing a 7.1% drop compared to previous years. According to data from LonRes, this marks the quietest September for property sales since 2016, with transactions falling by 16.8%. Achieved prices were also 8.2% below their pre-pandemic average, calculated on a price-per-square-foot basis. While there has been a slight recovery from the summer slowdown, the market continues to face significant pressure, with cautious buyers and widespread price reductions becoming the norm.

Sellers face significant discounts

In September, LonRes found that properties in prime London sold for an average of 10.1% below their original asking price. However, the extent of the discount varied depending on how long a property remained on the market. Homes that sold within three months achieved prices just 3.8% below their initial asking price during the third quarter. In contrast, properties that took between six and 12 months to sell required an average reduction of 11.1%. This highlights the importance of setting realistic prices from the outset to attract buyers more quickly.

Price reductions during the third quarter were 42.6% above the average seen between 2015 and 2024, indicating a challenging environment for sellers. Additionally, property withdrawals increased by 15.8% compared to the previous year, whilst new sales instructions fell by 13.2% annually. Despite this, the number of properties available for sale was 3.1% lower than a year earlier, suggesting a mixed picture for the market.

Super-prime market remains subdued

The super-prime market, encompassing properties priced above £5m, also continues to struggle despite a rise in new instructions. In September, new instructions for these high-value properties jumped by 32.5% compared to the previous year. However, transactions fell by 12.5% over the same period, reflecting ongoing uncertainty among discretionary buyers and sellers. Across the third quarter, £5m-plus sales declined by 9.3% annually, remaining 15.9% below the previous decade’s average. Price reductions in this segment were 88.8% above their long-term average, further emphasising the challenges faced by sellers in the luxury market.

Prime London rental market sees growth

Whilst sales prices declined, the prime lettings market recorded stronger rental growth in September. Average achieved rents increased by 4.6% annually, marking the fastest pace in 18 months. Rental values now stand 43.5% above their pre-pandemic average, highlighting the resilience of the lettings market. However, lettings activity weakened, with the number of lets agreed falling by 14.9% compared to the previous September.

The prime London property market remains in a state of flux, with sellers facing the need for significant price reductions to attract buyers. Meanwhile, the rental market continues to show strength, offering an alternative option for those navigating the current economic climate. Homeowners and prospective buyers may wish to carefully consider these trends when making decisions in this evolving market.

item.title: Overpriced homes struggle as buyers retreat ahead of Budget
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent figures and expert insights suggest that the UK housing market remains finely balanced, with buyers becoming increasingly selective amidst slowing price growth. According to the latest Office for National Statistics (ONS) data, annual house price growth eased to 0.9% in August, marking the weakest increase since March. With the average UK property now valued at £273,000, sellers may need to adjust their expectations to attract interest.

Realistic pricing key to attracting buyers

Nick Leeming, chairman of Jackson-Stops, noted that properties priced in line with recent comparable sales are continuing to draw serious interest. However, homes listed with overly ambitious price tags are facing a longer wait to secure a buyer. Leeming explained, “The market remains finely balanced. While there is still an appetite to move, buyers have considerable choice and are scrutinising value carefully.”

This trend is particularly evident in London, where the market continues to underperform. The capital recorded an annual price fall of 2.2%, with flats experiencing a sharper decline of 5%. For sellers in this segment, realistic pricing and presentation could prove crucial in securing a sale.

Budget uncertainty and higher mortgage rates weigh on activity

Richard Donnell, executive director of research at Zoopla, highlighted that higher mortgage rates and uncertainty ahead of the Autumn Budget are influencing buyer behaviour. “House price inflation is slowing as higher mortgage rates impact buyer enquiries and the number of sales agreed,” he said. Zoopla’s data indicates that fewer sales are taking place across the country as buyers adopt a wait-and-see approach.

Donnell added, “Homes that sell are doing so almost as quickly as last year, but buyers are becoming more selective, particularly when homes are not well presented or priced unrealistically.” For sellers, this underscores the importance of working closely with estate agents to understand how to appeal to serious buyers in the current market.

Speculation over property tax changes

Leeming also raised concerns about speculation surrounding potential property tax changes in the upcoming Budget. Reports suggesting that the government could lower the threshold for a proposed high-value council tax surcharge to £1.5m have added to uncertainty, particularly in higher-value markets. “Clarity and stability will be essential as we look ahead to the Budget,” Leeming said. “We hope speculation about changes to property taxation does not again delay decisions in these markets.”

As the market navigates these challenges, sellers may wish to focus on realistic pricing and presentation to attract buyers. With uncertainty looming ahead of the Budget, understanding local market trends and working with experienced agents could prove invaluable in achieving a successful sale.

item.title: Property industry braces for interest rate hike as mortgage deals disappear
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK property market is bracing for potential turbulence as economists predict an imminent interest rate rise by the Bank of England. With inflation remaining stubbornly high, many experts anticipate a hike in the base rate following the Monetary Policy Committee’s next meeting in November. This development could add further pressure to an already uncertain housing market, particularly for prospective buyers and homeowners seeking to refinance.

Mortgage Deals Disappear Amid Economic Uncertainty

Lenders have begun withdrawing some of their most competitive mortgage products, signalling a shift in the lending landscape. According to Propertymark, this trend reflects the growing economic uncertainty and its impact on affordability. Nathan Emerson, chief executive of Propertymark, noted that the housing market remains delicately balanced, with fluctuations in borrowing costs posing challenges for households. He highlighted that lenders are reacting swiftly to changing conditions, leaving prospective buyers with fewer options.

The withdrawal of mortgage deals comes at a time when households are already grappling with rising energy and food costs. For those looking to enter the property market or secure a new mortgage, affordability concerns are mounting. Borrowers may find it increasingly difficult to navigate the shifting landscape as lenders adjust their offerings in response to economic pressures.

November Rate Hike Likely as Inflation Persists

Economists have strengthened their predictions of an interest rate rise in November, with the latest inflation figures reinforcing these expectations. Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM, suggested that the data “almost guarantees” a hike, warning that inflation could exceed 4% early next year. This raises the possibility of further increases in the longer term, adding to the financial strain on households.

David Rees, head of global economics at Schroders, described the current economic climate as a “perfect storm of imported inflation pressures.” He indicated that a November rate hike now appears inevitable, echoing the sentiment shared by many industry experts. The Bank of England held rates at 3.75% in September, but three members of the Monetary Policy Committee voted for an increase, signalling growing support for tighter monetary policy.

Impact on the Housing Market

Higher interest rates could exacerbate affordability challenges, particularly for first-time buyers and those looking to remortgage. Buy-to-let investors may also face increased financing costs, potentially affecting rental yields and future property purchases. The extent to which mortgage pricing is impacted will depend on how much lenders have already factored in the anticipated rate rise.

For estate agents, the concern is whether rising borrowing costs will further dampen buyer confidence and slow market activity. With affordability already stretched, any additional pressure could lead to a cooling of demand. Homeowners and prospective buyers may wish to seek advice from mortgage brokers to explore their options and prepare for potential changes in the market.

As the Bank of England’s decision looms, the property industry remains on edge, navigating a landscape of uncertainty and shifting affordability dynamics.

item.title: Family launches DIY property platform to bypass estate agents
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

A new family-run property platform in Doncaster is offering homeowners and landlords an alternative to traditional estate agents by letting them handle their own sales and lettings. HownIt, created by Andrea Booth and her children, provides an online advertising space where users can list properties without paying estate agent fees, though they must manage the entire process themselves.

How the DIY property platform works

HownIt operates as an advertising platform rather than a full-service estate agency. Users create their own property listings, upload photographs and write descriptions, then communicate directly with potential buyers or tenants. Unlike traditional agents, the platform doesn’t arrange viewings, negotiate sales or handle legal work. Homeowners and landlords remain responsible for managing enquiries, organising property visits and progressing transactions independently.

The Booth family developed the idea after questioning estate agent fees during their own property transactions. Andrea Booth explained: “When selling my house, I kept wondering why the costs were so high.” The platform aims to give those confident in managing parts of the process a more affordable alternative to conventional agency services.

Current availability and future plans

Initially launching across Doncaster’s DN postcode area, HownIt is offering its first 30 users six months of free advertising, limited to one property per person. The company hasn’t yet revealed standard pricing or expansion plans beyond the trial period. This follows a growing trend of self-service property platforms that reduce fees by shifting responsibility to sellers and landlords.

Whilst these services can lower costs, they require users to handle tasks normally managed by professionals. Landlords should note that using such platforms doesn’t remove their legal obligations regarding tenant checks, safety certificates and other lettings requirements. Homeowners considering DIY property sales might wish to research conveyancing and negotiation processes beforehand to ensure smooth transactions.

As the property market evolves, services like HownIt demonstrate increasing appetite for alternatives to traditional estate agency models. However, prospective users should carefully weigh potential savings against the additional time and expertise required when managing sales or lettings independently.

item.title: Buy-to-let lending jumps 21% but landlord purchases fall
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK's buy-to-let mortgage market has seen a significant annual increase in lending during the second quarter of 2026, though analysts caution the figures may paint an overly optimistic picture. While total lending volumes rose by over 20% year-on-year, deeper analysis reveals a more nuanced situation for landlords.

Mixed picture for buy-to-let activity

New data from UK Finance shows £10.7 billion worth of buy-to-let mortgages were issued between April and June 2026, representing a 25% increase in value compared with the same period last year. The number of loans approved rose by 20.6% to 58,051. However, these apparently strong growth figures partly reflect unusually low activity in 2025, when landlords rushed to complete transactions ahead of stamp duty changes.

The market continues to be dominated by remortgaging rather than new purchases. Some 39,631 landlords opted to refinance their properties - an increase of 17.6% annually and 470 more than in the previous quarter. By contrast, new purchases declined slightly quarter-on-quarter, with just 16,026 mortgages for property acquisitions, suggesting existing investors are focusing on managing current portfolios rather than expanding them.

Rental yields stable despite cost pressures

Average gross rental yields remained virtually unchanged at 7.27%, demonstrating continued resilience in the private rented sector. However, landlords faced modest increases in borrowing costs, with average interest rates on new buy-to-let loans rising to 4.82% from 4.70% in the first quarter. Despite this, rates remain below their level from a year earlier.

The average interest cover ratio - which measures rental income against mortgage payments - improved slightly to 217%, compared with 210% in Q2 2025. This suggests that while costs have risen, landlords are generally maintaining comfortable buffers.

Arrears show positive trend

The sector saw further improvement in mortgage arrears, with 8,390 buy-to-let loans reported as being in significant arrears (exceeding 2.5% of the outstanding balance) at the end of June. This represents a 25.6% annual reduction and a decrease of 570 cases compared with the previous quarter.

Possessions also declined, with lenders recording 630 cases during the quarter - 20.3% fewer than a year earlier. The number of outstanding fixed-rate buy-to-let mortgages fell by 0.7% to 1.46 million, while variable-rate products declined by 3% to 450,000.

Industry experts advise caution when interpreting the annual growth figures, noting that comparisons with 2025's unusually low lending levels may exaggerate the market's current strength. With economic uncertainty continuing and borrowing costs remaining elevated, landlords might consider reviewing their portfolios and financing arrangements to ensure they remain sustainable.

item.title: £1.4bn investment portfolios available for sale
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research from Rushbrook has revealed 1,322 property investment portfolios currently available for purchase across England, with a combined value exceeding £1.4 billion. The findings highlight significant opportunities for portfolio investors, particularly in the capital where London-based properties account for nearly a third of the total market value.

Regional Breakdown of Available Portfolios

The research provides a detailed geographical analysis of investment opportunities across England:

  • London represents the highest concentration by value, with portfolios worth approximately £460 million
  • The South East follows with around £320 million worth of portfolio listings
  • Northern regions collectively account for nearly £280 million of available investments
  • The Midlands offers portfolios valued at roughly £200 million

This distribution suggests that while London dominates in terms of individual property values, substantial investment potential exists throughout England. Property investors might consider regional variations in yields and capital growth prospects when evaluating these opportunities.

What Portfolio Investors Should Consider

For those contemplating purchasing a property portfolio, several factors could be worth evaluating:

  • Portfolio composition – whether it consists of residential, commercial or mixed property types
  • Current tenancy arrangements and rental income streams
  • Local market conditions in the portfolio's geographical area
  • Mortgage financing options for portfolio purchases
  • Potential for value-add through refurbishment or management improvements

Portfolio investors may wish to seek specialist mortgage advice, as financing multiple properties often involves different criteria compared to single buy-to-let purchases. Lenders typically assess the overall strength of the portfolio rather than individual properties when making lending decisions.

With £1.4 billion worth of portfolios currently on the market, investors have substantial choice across England. However, thorough due diligence remains essential when considering any property investment opportunity.
